newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran anti-drug war on right track-U.N. official.
newsitem.headline: Iran anti-drug war on right track-U.N. official.

text.p: Iran maintains a high success rate in seizing opium smuggled from Afghanistan and Pakistan on camels and in four-wheel drive vehicles on its way to world markets, a United Nations official said on Tuesday.

Giovanni Quaglia, director of the U.N. International Drug Control Programme (UNDCP) for southwest Asia, said Iran last year seized 300 tonnes of opium out of the 2,300 produced in neighbouring Afghanistan, one of the world's biggest suppliers.
"Confiscating 12 to 13 percent of what is produced is the highest percentage in the world in a single country," he told Reuters by telephone from Tehran.
"Had we had similar success in other countries we would have good progress in the drug control field," he said. "In Europe only five percent of what is smuggled is confiscated."
Quaglia, who is based in Islamabad, is visiting Iran which on Tuesday marks anti-drugs day. Authorities will later in the day burn 45 tonnes of drugs near Tehran in a public ceremony.
Iran is a key transit route for drugs, mostly opium from which heroin is made, being smuggled to Europe via Turkey from Afghanistan and Pakistan -- the so-called "Golden Crescent".

Diplomats say the Islamic republic -- which imposes the death penalty for drug possession -- appears to be intensifying its crackdown, but that its rugged borders and the highly professional smuggling operation made the task daunting.
Iranian officials say Iran's anti-drugs policy has not halted shipments of drugs through its territory because of a lack of cooperation by regional states.

On Monday, Iran's Interior Minister Mohammad Besharati said in Tehran that Iran's efforts alone were not enough. "Taking into account the fact that Iran is neighbouring Afghanistan and Pakistan, the investment made by Iran is insufficient. The anti-drug campaign in Iran requires international assistance."
The amount of drugs that made it through Iran to international markets was not clear, the diplomats said.

But Quaglia said that of the opium produced in Afghanistan, about 1,000 tonnes were consumed in Afghanistan, Pakistan and Iran, 300 confiscated and the remaining 1,000 tonnes converted into morphine and heroin for the world market, mostly Europe.
Iranian officials estimate there are one million drug addicts in the country.

Iran said last week it had erected barbed wire fences, dug trenches, and set up hundreds of checkpoints and watchtowers along its borders to prevent traffickers entering its territory. It said it planned to plant mines on routes used by smugglers.
Quaglia said part of Iran's success in seizing drugs was having a good "intelligence system". He said Iran also spent $200 million in the last two years on border fortifications.
"Every 10 km (six miles) they erected observation posts and built a route connecting them on the 1,200 km (745 mile) border with Afghanistan and the 1,000 km (620 mile) one with Pakistan."

But "the traffickers are well organised and professional. They are heavily armed even with anti-helicopter missiles and high-speed vehicles," Quaglia said. "They come in camel caravans, in four-wheel drive vehicles and hide drugs in lorries. They do their best to avoid observation."
Iran said it seized 175 tonnes (385,800 lb) of narcotics and arrested 16,000 dealers in the year to March 1997. In the previous year it seized 170 tonnes, officials said.

According to Iranian law, possession of five kg (11 lb) of opium or 30 grams of heroin is punishable by death. More than 1,000 people have been executed in drug-related cases since the law took effect in 1989.
Officials said last week that nearly six out of every 10 convicts held in the country's jails were drugs offenders.
Besharati said 200 policemen were killed and 500 injured in clashes with armed drug traffickers in the past four years.
